propositions.text: The claimant is a Chinese citizen claiming refugee protection under sections 96 and 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act.
propositions.quote: XXX XXX XXXX (the "claimant") is a citizen of China who claims refugee protection pursuant to section 96 and 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (the "Act").1

paragraphs.summary: The claimant is a Chinese citizen claiming refugee protection under the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, says the court.

propositions.text: The claimant fears persecution because of his religious practices.
propositions.quote: The claimant fears persecution because of his religious practices.

paragraphs.summary: The claimant alleges he fears persecution due to his religious practices.

propositions.text: In 2004, the claimant met his devout Catholic wife and started attending an underground Roman Catholic Church.
propositions.quote: In 2004, he met his current wife, XXXX XXX XXXX, a devout Catholic. They started to attend services at an underground Roman Catholic Church.

propositions.text: The claimant was baptized in 2005.
propositions.quote: The claimant was baptized in XXXX 2005.

paragraphs.summary: The claimant met his Catholic wife in 2004, attended underground church, and was baptized in 2005, according to the claimant.

propositions.text: The claimant married his wife in 2006 and continued attending Bible classes.
propositions.quote: In XXXX 2006, the claimant married his wife. He continued to attend Bible classes.

paragraphs.summary: The claimant married in 2006 and continued Bible study, says the claimant.

propositions.text: In 2007, police questioned the claimant about anti-government activity and warned him of surveillance.
propositions.quote: In XXXX 2007, a police officer questioned the claimant about whether he was part of an anti-government organization, and warned him that he was under surveillance.

propositions.text: The claimant and friends suspended their Bible study group temporarily, resuming in 2008.
propositions.quote: The claimant and his friends decided to suspend their Bible study group for a while. It resumed meetings in XXXX 2008.

paragraphs.summary: The claimant says police questioned him in 2007, leading to a temporary suspension of Bible study, which resumed in 2008.

propositions.text: In 2008, police broke up a Bible study group at the claimant's house and arrested worshippers.
propositions.quote: In XXXX 2008, a Bible study group being hosted in the claimant's house was broken up by the police, who arrested the worshippers.

paragraphs.summary: The claimant states police broke up a Bible study at his home in 2008 and arrested participants.

propositions.text: The claimant was detained, questioned, threatened, assaulted, pressured to confess, and released with conditions including no religious activities and weekly police reporting.
propositions.quote: The claimant was detained, questioned, threatened, and assaulted. He was pressured to write a confession. He was released on conditions including refraining from religious activities and reporting weekly to the police.

paragraphs.summary: The claimant alleges detention with mistreatment and conditional release forbidding religious activities and requiring police reporting.

propositions.text: The claimant and wife decided to leave China; he traveled to Singapore and Malaysia but was told he could not claim refugee status there.
propositions.quote: The claimant and his wife decided that they should leave China. The claimant was able to book himself into a tour of Singapore and Malaysia. His wife could not join him as she did not have a passport. He went to police stations in both Singapore and Malaysia and was advised that he could not make refugee claims.

paragraphs.summary: The claimant says he tried to leave China via Singapore and Malaysia but was told refugee claims were not possible there.

propositions.text: Upon return to China, the claimant learned his wife was arrested, so he went into hiding and arranged exit with an agent's help.
propositions.quote: Upon returning to China, via the Hong Kong airport, the claimant learned that his wife had been arrested. Therefore, he went into hiding until he was able to arrange exit with the help of an agent.

paragraphs.summary: The claimant states he hid after his wife's arrest and arranged to leave China with an agent's help.

propositions.text: The claimant entered Canada in 2009 and made a refugee claim on April 20, 2009.
propositions.quote: He entered Canada on XXXX, 2009 and made a refugee claim on April 20, 2009.

paragraphs.summary: The claimant entered Canada in 2009 and filed a refugee claim on April 20, 2009.

propositions.text: The claimant's wife remains in jail.
propositions.quote: His wife remains in jail.

paragraphs.summary: The claimant states his wife remains imprisoned.

propositions.text: The claimant is not a Convention refugee as he lacks a well-founded fear of persecution for a Convention ground in China.
propositions.quote: I find that the claimant is not a Convention refugee in that he does not have a well-founded fear of persecution for a Convention ground in China.

propositions.text: The claimant is not a person in need of protection as removal to China would not risk his life, cruel treatment, or torture.
propositions.quote: I also find that the claimant is not a person in need of protection in that his removal to China would not subject him personally to a risk to his life or to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, and in that there are no substantial grounds to believe that his removal to China would subject him personally to a danger of torture.

propositions.text: The court will provide reasons for these findings.
propositions.quote: My reasons are as follows.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the claimant is neither a Convention refugee nor in need of protection and will explain reasons.

propositions.text: The claimant's identity is established by his passport copy in evidence.
propositions.quote: The personal identity of the claimant is established by the copy of his passport2 that is in evidence.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the claimant's identity established by his passport copy.

propositions.text: Sworn testimony is presumed true unless there is sufficient reason to doubt it.
propositions.quote: there is a presumption that sworn testimony is true unless there is sufficient reason to doubt its truthfulness.

propositions.text: The claimant's evidence raises concerns about its reliability.
propositions.quote: In this claim, the evidence raises a number of concerns about its reliability.

paragraphs.summary: The court presumes sworn testimony true but finds concerns about the claimant's evidence reliability.

propositions.text: At hearing start, the claimant amended his Personal Information Form, changing his employment history from that in his Canadian Visitor Visa application.
propositions.quote: At the start of the hearing, the claimant amended his Personal Information Form, replacing the stated employment history. That history had been consistent with the information provided in his application for a Canadian Visitor Visa (CVV).3

propositions.text: The claimant allegedly obtained the CVV through an agent and the CVV contained a false employment history.
propositions.quote: The claimant allegedly obtained the CVV through the services of an agent and contained a false employment history.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes the claimant changed his Personal Information Form employment history, which was consistent with a CVV application containing false employment history.

propositions.text: Changing employment history makes the PIF more consistent with fear-based agent use but shows willingness to sign false statements.
propositions.quote: The effect of changing the employment history is that the Personal Information Form (PIF)4 is now more consistent with the allegation that, due to fear, he used an agent to help him leave China. It is therefore a material difference. However, the change of information also demonstrates that the claimant is willing to sign his name to false statements.

propositions.text: The original PIF had handwritten corrections showing claimant's awareness of untrue information.
propositions.quote: The PIF as originally provided, already shows handwritten corrections to the employment history, demonstrating that he had been aware of the information that he was providing to the Board, which he now states is untrue.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the claimant's employment history change is material but shows willingness to sign false statements, with original PIF corrections.

propositions.text: Claimant's passport shows Singapore and Canadian visas in 2009, inconsistent with his claim of hiding between 2008 and 2009.
propositions.quote: However, according to the information in his passport, he obtained a Singaporean visa in XXXX in XXXX 2009 and a Canadian visa in Beijing in XXXX 2009. This is not suggestive of hiding.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds passport visa dates contradict claimant's claim of hiding in 2008-2009.

propositions.text: Claimant's garbled, slow, hesitant recitation of prayers is understandable due to interpreter but inconsistent with years of Bible study.
propositions.quote: His recitations were rather garbled, which is quite understandable given the use of an interpreter. They were also very slowly and hesitantly delivered, which is harder to understand, given his alleged Bible study of several years.

propositions.text: Claimant confused Communion with baptism but knew religious significance of Christmas and Easter.
propositions.quote: I also note that, while he could cite the religious significance of Christmas and Easter, he confused Communion with baptism.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds claimant's hesitant prayer recitations and confusion about Communion inconsistent with his Bible study claim.

propositions.text: Claimant testified never officially baptized and does not take Communion despite weekly church attendance in Canada, inconsistent with prior claims.
propositions.quote: Indeed, he testified that he has never been officially baptized and does not take Communion despite attending weekly church services in Canada. This testimony is inconsistent with the commitment implicit in his alleged attendance at and hosting of Bible study meetings even after the police told him to desist.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds claimant's testimony about baptism and Communion inconsistent with his alleged religious commitment.

propositions.text: Claimant's alleged violent detention and wife's ongoing detention are inconsistent with country documents on treatment of Catholics and unregistered church worshippers.
propositions.quote: A fourth concern is that the violent treatment allegedly given to the claimant in detention, and the ongoing detention of his wife, is inconsistent with some of the country documentation regarding the treatment of similarly situated persons, that is, Catholics and/or worshippers at unregistered churches.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds claimant's allegations of violent detention and wife's imprisonment inconsistent with country documents on treatment of similar persons.

propositions.text: Relationship between Chinese government and Vatican has improved; bishops seek Vatican approval; state allows religious beliefs but arrests and surveillance continue.
propositions.quote: One report5 states that the relationship between the Chinese government and the Vatican has greatly improved over the last few years. Most, if not all, Chinese bishops appointed by the government-sanctioned Catholic association also seek Vatican approval. The state has officially given approval to the holding of religious beliefs, although there are still arrests and surveillance on underground churches.

propositions.text: Source says nothing about routine violence against church members.
propositions.quote: This source says nothing about the routine employment of violence against church members, however.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker reports improved China-Vatican relations, some religious freedom, but no routine violence against church members.

propositions.text: US Department of State says unregistered church members use legal avenues to practice faith, deterring harassment.
propositions.quote: In another document,6 the US Department of State indicates that unregistered church members pursue their right to practice their faith through legal avenues, which have helped deter harassment from local authorities.

propositions.text: Canadian lawyer disputes this view; document not unequivocally optimistic about religious freedom in China.
propositions.quote: I note that this view is disputed by a Canadian lawyer quoted in the same document, so this document is not being interpreted as giving an unequivocally optimistic opinion of religious freedom in China.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker notes US report on legal religious practice but also a Canadian lawyer's dispute, so religious freedom view is not fully optimistic.

propositions.text: Board report states about 14 million Catholics in China, some arrested and fined, others experience tolerance.
propositions.quote: A more recent Board report7 states that there are about 14 million registered and unregistered Catholics in the country. One source indicates that Catholics can be arrested and fined, while another source states that there is a high degree of tolerance.

propositions.text: Authorities in Guangdong and Fujian provinces might be more tolerant to Catholics than other provinces.
propositions.quote: Several sources have stated that they believe that authorities in Guangdong (where the claimant is from) and Fujian provinces might be more tolerant to Catholics than in other provinces.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker reports mixed treatment of Catholics and possible greater tolerance in claimant's home provinces.

propositions.text: Documents show inconsistent harassment of clergy and worshippers, some tolerance, little support for claimant's allegations of beatings and indefinite detention of wife.
propositions.quote: In sum, the documents show that there is harassment of clergy and some worshippers, inconsistently applied, but also indications of tolerance, and little support overall for the allegations of being beaten and for the indefinite detention of the claimant's wife.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker finds inconsistent harassment and little support for claimant's allegations of beatings and wife's detention.

propositions.text: There is very little evidence that the claimant is actually married to his wife, who inspires his religious persecution claim.
propositions.quote: The fifth concern is that there is very little evidence that the claimant is actually married to his wife, the inspiration behind the religious activities that give rise to his alleged fear of persecution.

paragraphs.summary: The court identifies little evidence that claimant is married to the wife central to his persecution claim.

propositions.text: Claimants are not obligated to provide corroborative evidence but should submit it if they possess or can obtain it.
propositions.quote: While there is no obligation that claimants provide corroborative documentation of their allegations, it is reasonable to expect that claimants who possess or could readily obtain such evidence would submit it for their hearings.

paragraphs.summary: The court states claimants need not provide corroboration but should if they have or can get it.

propositions.text: Claimant married wife in 2006, lived with retired parents; no photos or notes presented; materials allegedly seized by authorities.
propositions.quote: The claimant has allegedly known his wife since 2004, married her in 2006, and lived with her in the home of his retired parents. He has presented no photos, cards or notes from his wife. The claimant states that all of these materials were seized by the authorities for no reason.

propositions.text: Marriage circumstances odd: claimant's parents and adult daughter not present at wedding.
propositions.quote: The circumstances of the marriage are odd, in that the claimant's parents and adult daughter were not present at the wedding.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes claimant's marriage details, lack of evidence, and odd wedding circumstances.

propositions.text: Claimant's wife listed in Canadian Visitor Visa application, but claimant admitted false employment statements there.
propositions.quote: The claimant's wife is listed in his application for a Canadian Visitor Visa (CVV), but, as already noted, he has admitted to making false employment statements in this document.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes claimant's wife is listed on visa application, but claimant admitted false statements there.

propositions.text: Claimant brought untranslated hukou document; household register is primary ID in China listing all household occupants.
propositions.quote: The claimant brought an untranslated document to the hearing, which he identified as his hukou, or household registration. The country document package indicates that the household register is a primary identification document in China which is issued by the police. There is legal obligation to list all of the occupants of the household.8

paragraphs.summary: The court describes claimant's hukou document as primary ID listing all household occupants.

propositions.text: Translation shows household occupants include claimant's family but not his supposed wife; document issued 1998, updated 2010.
propositions.quote: A translation of the document at the hearing revealed that the household occupants consisted of the claimant's father (head of household), mother, the claimant, his two brothers, a sister-in-law, and a nephew. The hukou was issued on XXXX, 1998, and updated on XXXX, 2010. The claimant's supposed wife is not listed in it.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds claimant's wife is not listed in the hukou document despite updates.

propositions.text: Claimant first says wife's absence from hukou is usual; then changes explanation to provincial differences; says wife lived with him and parents since 2005 and 2009 respectively.
propositions.quote: The claimant's explanation for the absence of his wife from the document is that this is quite usual in China. When told that our country information indicates otherwise, he changed his explanation, stating that it is a problem for couples who initially come from different provinces to obtain accurate updates to their hukou. He averred that his wife lived with him from 2005, and that she is currently living with his parents and has been there since 2009.

paragraphs.summary: The court recounts claimant's inconsistent explanations for wife's absence from hukou.

propositions.text: Claimant's testimony about wife's whereabouts is inconsistent with his allegation that she remains in jail, raising a credibility concern.
propositions.quote: Aside from there being no documentary foundation for either explanation, the claimant's answer raises a sixth credibility concern, which is that his testimony about his wife's whereabouts is utterly inconsistent with the allegation, stated in the PIF and never amended, that his wife "remains in jail."

paragraphs.summary: The court finds claimant's testimony about wife's location inconsistent with his claim she is jailed, harming credibility.

propositions.text: This inconsistency is highly material; presumption of truthfulness overcome; claimant is not a reliable witness.
propositions.quote: This is a highly material inconsistency, since his flight from China was supposedly triggered by his wife's jailing and ongoing incarceration. On the evidence, I find that the presumption of truthfulness has been overcome. The claimant is not a reliable witness.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds claimant not credible due to material inconsistency about wife's incarceration.

propositions.text: Court considered whether other evidence could support claimant's protection claim.
propositions.quote: I have considered whether there is other evidence that could support his claim for protection.

paragraphs.summary: The court considered if other evidence supports claimant's protection claim.

propositions.text: Documentation shows claimant attends church activities in Canada but does not address experiences in China.
propositions.quote: There is documentation9 that the claimant attends church activities in Canada, but this does not address his experiences in China.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes claimant's church attendance in Canada but no evidence about China experiences.

propositions.text: Claimant submitted mobile phone statement after hearing; relevant but little probative value due to lack of verification and claimant's lack of credibility.
propositions.quote: After the hearing, counsel for the claimant submitted a document purporting to be a mobile phone statement, billed to XXXX XXX XXXX at the claimant's address in XXXX City. This document is relevant. However, it has very little probative value, since it is a paper document issued by a private company, without any verification of its issuance, and provided by the claimant, who is not credible.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds claimant's submitted phone statement has little probative value due to lack of verification and claimant's non-credibility.

propositions.text: Insufficient trustworthy evidence to analyze protection claim; no basis for positive finding under IRPA sections 96 or 97(1).
propositions.quote: In sum, there is insufficient trustworthy and reliable evidence upon which I could analyze a claim for protection. Accordingly, there is no basis upon which I can make a positive finding under either section 96 or section 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes there is insufficient reliable evidence to grant protection under IRPA sections 96 or 97(1).

propositions.text: Claimant is not a Convention refugee or person in need of protection; claim is rejected.
propositions.quote: For the foregoing reasons, I conclude that XXX XXXX XXXX is not a Convention refugee and not a person in need of protection and I therefore reject his claim.

paragraphs.summary: The court rejects claimant's claim, finding he is not a refugee or person in need of protection.
